practice1.prompt: Write has_duplicate(items): return True if any value appears more than once, False otherwise. One pass over the list, no loop inside a loop.

cases.name: answers correctly for any list

hiddenCases.name: still right when nearly everything repeats
one pass, not a loop inside a loop
hiddenCases.describe: has_duplicate(items) that walks the list once

practice1.hint: Comparing every item against every other item gives the right answer and is the slow answer. The lesson's optimisation tips name the data structure that lets you ask "have I seen this already" without a second loop.

questions.prompt: What is the complexity of a loop nested inside another loop over the same list?
questions.explain: The inner loop runs about n times for each of the n turns of the outer one. At n = 1000 that is a million steps rather than a thousand.

questions.prompt: Why is `item in my_set` usually faster than `item in my_list`?
choices: Sets are stored in order, so the search can stop early
A set looks the value up directly, O(1), while a list may check every element, O(n)
questions.explain: That single swap is what turns the lesson's O(n^2) duplicate finder into an O(n) one. The loop structure changed because the lookup cost changed.

questions.prompt: Match each complexity to an operation that has it.
right: Binary search over a sorted list
Comparing every pair in a list
questions.explain: Big-O describes how the work grows with the input, not how long any one run takes. Indexing is one step whether the list holds ten items or ten million.

questions.prompt: In Big-O notation, the letter ___ stands for the size of the input.
questions.explain: Everything in the notation is written relative to that size, which is why constants and smaller terms get dropped: they stop mattering as n grows.

questions.prompt: Which of these usually make code faster on large inputs?
choices: Using a set instead of a list for membership tests
Storing a value you computed rather than recomputing it
Replacing a nested loop with a single pass
questions.explain: The first three change how much work is done. Variable names change nothing at run time; they are compiled away.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Say what Big-O measures, then give one operation whose cost does not change with the input and one whose cost grows with it.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Efficiency rarely matters on five items. Say what changes when the same code meets a lot of data.
